item.title: Are New Parties Shut Out of the UK House of Commons?
item.description: arXiv:2610.28866v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In recent years it has been claimed that new political parties are shut out of the UK House of Commons because they are rarely elected. At the same time, general political understanding seems to be that the House of Commons is currently further away from a pure two-party distribution of seats than at any time in the past century, perhaps longer. Although this might seem like a paradox it is possible for both of these things to have credence. We present an analysis that shows that the number of new political parties elected to the House of Commons has been slowly declining over the last century. We illustrate this both by regression and Good-Turing analyses. We also analyse the lifetime and persistence of political parties as well as present metrics that indicate the recent increased political diversity and identify the nadir of diversity in the mid-1960s and early 1970s.
item.dc:creator: Guy P. Nason

item.title: Dual-Phase Flow Matching for Probabilistic Source Detection and Measurement in Astronomical Images
item.description: arXiv:2610.28919v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Using the largest digital camera ever built, the NSF-DOE Vera C. Rubin Observatory's 10-year Legacy Survey of Space and Time (LSST) will image over half the night sky. Most astronomical analyses of LSST data operate not on images but on catalogs derived from them: tables of light sources detailing their positions, fluxes (colors and brightnesses), and types (e.g., star, galaxy). At LSST's imaging depths, light sources often overlap visually, so the configuration of sources in each image is itself uncertain. Nevertheless, LSST's cataloging pipeline commits to a single source configuration, which can bias downstream analyses. Here, we instead approximate a posterior distribution over source configurations. Our posterior approximation is a continuous-time Markov process (CTMP) fitted by generator matching, an extension of flow matching to non-Euclidean state spaces. This CTMP generates a source configuration in two phases: it detects light sources in the first and measures them in the second. On simulated LSST-like data, the proposed method produces better posterior approximations than five comparison methods: two Markov chain Monte Carlo methods that run thousands of times more slowly at survey scales; two neural posterior estimation methods; and one ablation of the proposed method that lacks the dual-phase structure. Applied to LSST Data Preview 1 (DP1), the first public release of Rubin imaging, the proposed method alone recovers small-scale galaxy clustering in agreement with higher-resolution Hubble imaging and reports uncertainty that remains calibrated against that reference as blending increases. We deliver a probabilistic catalog of the Extended Chandra Deep Field South region, one of the most extensively studied extragalactic fields, and use it to characterize the galaxy color-magnitude distribution.
item.dc:creator: Yicun Duan, Jeffrey Regier

item.title: Generalized survival energy models with exogenous covariates for mortality prediction
item.description: arXiv:2610.29002v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We develop a generalized survival energy model that relates mortality to social and economic conditions through a latent energy process. Death occurs when this process first reaches or crosses zero. Environmental covariates enter the coefficients governing depletion, recovery, fluctuations and accumulated damage, yielding lifetime distributions conditional on the environmental path. We derive these distributions for diffusion and inverse Gaussian specifications and describe their numerical evaluation. An application to Japanese male and female mortality data assesses predictive performance against Cairns--Blake--Dowd benchmarks. Conditional on realized environmental paths, the selected inverse Gaussian models achieve small prediction errors comparable to those of the benchmarks. The framework also provides a model-based interpretation of how environmental changes affect mortality through the rate of damage accumulation or the magnitude of energy fluctuations. These interpretations describe conditional statistical relationships rather than causal effects. The resulting models offer a way to study mortality under alternative environmental scenarios while retaining a connection to classical actuarial survival models.
item.dc:creator: Yasutaka Shimizu

item.title: Flowz: When Does Learning Forecast Errors Add Value? Conditional Flow Matching for Financial Price Forecasts
item.description: arXiv:2610.29991v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Learning a forecasting model's errors offers a modular way to improve its predictive distribution while retaining its underlying dynamics. We study this approach with Flowz, a conditional flow model of direct multi-step price-level residuals fitted using random features and ridge regression. Each EWMA, ARIMA, ARFIMA, and structural baseline is compared with a Gaussian residual location-scale control and a conditional Flowz extension. The experiment uses 24 US stocks selected across four liquidity-volatility strata, 104 common forecast origins, horizons of 5, 10, 20, 40, 80, and 160 trading observations, and three fit seeds. Marginal CRPS is the primary score. At farther horizons, Flowz reduces mean CRPS by 30.7% against EWMA and 24.0% against its Gaussian residual control. The EWMA improvement holds at each fit seed and exceeds the Gaussian control for all 24 stocks in the far band. The ARIMA, ARFIMA, and structural extensions worsen both comparators. Conditional residual learning is therefore useful for the drifting EWMA specification in this experiment, with gains concentrated at longer horizons.
item.dc:creator: Giancarlo Vercellino

item.title: Technical Report: Causal ANOVA Applied to COMPAS
item.description: arXiv:2610.30110v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This report applies Causal ANOVA to the COMPAS recidivism prediction dataset to study how demographic variables contribute to variation in two-year recidivism outcomes. Using a directed acyclic graph (DAG) to encode causal assumptions, we estimate counterfactual explainability scores for Race, Sex, and Age Category. We then examine whether the explanatory roles of Race and Sex change after conditioning on age group. The results suggest that Age Category explains the largest share of variation in the full causal model. After conditioning on age, Sex explainability is highest among younger defendants and declines with age, while Race explainability increases with age and is most pronounced among older defendants. As a complementary analysis, we use logistic regression models to interpret the demographic patterns suggested by the Causal ANOVA results. We provide a Python package of Causal ANOVA at https://github.com/devonxiong/causal-anova.
item.dc:creator: Yiming Xiong, Zijun Gao

item.title: Learning Checklists to Reduce Lottery Effects in Scientific Peer Review
item.description: arXiv:2610.28666v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Reviewer lottery error describes error due to a small set of peer reviews attending to only some of the issues with a paper that a larger pool of eligible reviewers would raise. We show this error can be reduced by surfacing a checklist of criticisms learned from a historical review corpus. Our approach generates a tree of checklists representing coarsenings of the atomic review claim space, then selects the coarsening that maximizes a theoretically-motivated measure of correlated agreement among reviewers. We realize this approach with an LLM-assisted pipeline and test it on NeurIPS 2021 and ICLR 2022 review data. In simulated review with LLM reviewers, the learned checklist reduces the mean squared error (MSE) of a three reviewer committee by 58% on NeurIPS and 21% on ICLR, and on both venues the checklist with the highest correlated agreement has the lowest error for committees of three or more. In a human study with 20 participants, the learned NeurIPS checklist lowers the MSE of a paper ranking, measured against the NeurIPS 2021 order, from 0.48 to 0.22.
item.dc:creator: Xuanyou Liu, Ziyang Guo, Jason Hartline, Jessica Hullman

item.title: Calibration scoring under dependent seed variables in Cooke's Classical Model: a Mehler-Hermite design-effect correction
item.description: arXiv:2610.28831v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Cooke's Classical Model scores the statistical accuracy of experts by the $p$-value of a likelihood ratio test that compares the bin frequencies of realized seed variables with nominal probabilities, using a $\chi^2$ reference. This calibration score drives performance-based weights and implicitly assumes independent seed variables, although seeds often share a common driver, such as the same indicator in several regions or periods. Under dependence the statistic converges to a weighted sum of $\chi^2_1$ variables, and positive dependence makes the classical score anti-conservative. Under a Gaussian-copula working model, a Mehler-Hermite expansion gives the long-run covariance of the bin indicators in closed form, defines a design effect and an effective number of seed variables, and shows that the first-order correction coincides with the ad hoc calibration power of existing software. Rao-Scott-type and parametric-bootstrap corrected scores are proposed, together with a restricted maximum likelihood estimator of the nuisance dependence, computed from rank normal scores and invariant to location-scale miscalibration, and a prepivoted bootstrap that propagates its uncertainty. In simulations the classical score rejects up to 68\% of calibrated experts at a nominal 5\% level, whereas the corrected scores remove most of the excess rejection. In 45 published studies, design effects of 1.25-2 shift more than 5\% of the optimized weight in 29-44\% of studies. In three social-science studies with structured seeds, the baseline estimates imply that 18-21 seed variables carry the information of only 11-13 independent ones, although conclusions about individual experts depend on how the dependence is specified.
item.dc:creator: Yuri Calleo

item.title: Anytime-Valid Inference in Conjoint Experiments
item.description: arXiv:2610.28979v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Choosing an appropriate sample size is a fundamental challenge in experimental design. This challenge is particularly salient in conjoint experiments, where researchers simultaneously target many estimands whose inferential goals may be reached at different sample sizes. Conventional sample-size calculations address this challenge in an ex ante manner. In large online studies, including many conjoint experiments, data often arrive continuously, allowing researchers to dynamically stop data collection. In such settings, the relevant practical question is not "what sample size should I choose in advance?" but rather, as data accumulate, "have I learned enough yet?" A naive response is to repeatedly inspect conventional confidence intervals and $p$-values, but doing so invalidates their inferential guarantees. We address this challenge by developing a general anytime-valid framework for conjoint experiments that allows continuous monitoring and data-dependent stopping. This framework equips many common conjoint estimands with asymptotic $e$-processes, confidence sequences, and anytime-valid $p$-values, and provides a general recipe for any estimand that can be expressed as a linear contrast of population OLS coefficients. Across common conjoint settings, we demonstrate that anytime-valid inference can yield substantial sample savings relative to fixed-sample designs. The probability of early stopping frequently exceeds 50%, with mean sample savings often surpassing 25%.
item.dc:creator: Daniel Molitor, Jennah Gosciak, Michael Lindon

item.title: StochIKM: Automated High-Fidelity Reconstruction of Individual Patient Data from Published Kaplan-Meier Curves
item.description: arXiv:2610.29122v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Individual patient data are the gold standard for secondary analysis of time-to-event evidence, but they are rarely released, and reconstruction from a published Kaplan-Meier figure could help. Existing methods all claim high fidelity, each judged by whichever agreements it happens to achieve, and each returns a single dataset although the map from figure to data is not bijective. We define fidelity explicitly: a dataset is admissible when it reproduces the risk table exactly, follows the digitized curve to within the image resolution, and respects the printed median, interval and event count. We propose StochIKM, a stochastic algorithm that digitizes the figure with a vision-capable language model and uses the high-fidelity definition as constraints, returning an admissible set of individual patient datasets. A solution is guaranteed to exist whenever the figure has been read correctly, so a failure indicts either the published figure or its digitization. In simulation and in 79 arms from published oncology trials, StochIKM reproduces the published risk tables and medians more closely than LLM-improved IPDfromKM, a high-impact alternative.
item.dc:creator: Liangze Ke, Daniel Zelterman, Wei Wei, Guannan Gong

item.title: Using Temporal Replication and Partial Pooling to Improve Practical Identifiability in Presence-Only Poisson Point Process Models
item.description: arXiv:2610.29365v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Species distribution models based on thinned point processes are now commonly used in ecology to analyze presence-only data collected through citizen science, including in spatio-temporal frameworks. A key challenge in these models is the separation of the ecological process from the observation process, which raises identifiability issues. Here, we investigate the theoretical and practical identifiability of a thinned Poisson point process model. We show that, with a log link for ecological intensity and a logit link for observation probability, the model can be structurally identifiable under simple conditions, provided that observation probability varies spatially. We then evaluate the benefits of using temporal replication within a spatio-temporal framework to improve estimation when ecological intensity and observation probability are weakly separated. We quantify these benefits through simulations. The results highlight persistent practical identifiability problems affecting the ecological and observation intercepts, especially when observation probabilities are low. However, in a spatio-temporal model with partial pooling, these parameters are estimated more accurately than in a single-year model, even when only a short time period is considered. Temporal replication also improves estimation of parameters shared across years. Finally, we illustrate the use of such a spatio-temporal model through a study of coypu (Myocastor coypus) distribution in Occitanie, France. Overall, our results show that temporal replication can partially alleviate practical identifiability problems in presence-only point process models when independent data sources are unavailable.
item.dc:creator: Camille Mottier (Institut Montpelli\'erain Alexander Grothendieck, Centre d'\'Ecologie Fonctionnelle et \'Evolutive), Iris Lang (Conservatoire d'espaces naturels Occitanie), Justine Nicolas (Conservatoire d'espaces naturels Occitanie), Olivier Gimenez (Centre d'\'Ecologie Fonctionnelle et \'Evolutive)

item.title: Bayesian Comparison of Covid Origins Hypotheses
item.description: arXiv:2610.29766v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Applying standard Bayesian methods to the most reliably known unclassified facts about the Covid epidemic allows crude estimation of the odds for research-related vs. purely zoonotic origins. Here a broadly inclusive zoonotic hypothesis is compared with a rather specific subset of the research-related hypothesis defined by known prior work and grant proposals. The important observations are the type of virus, the city of the first outbreak, the lack of known prior hosts, the anomalous early pattern of evolution, and two specific features of the viral sequence. The resulting odds strongly favor research. The odds remain fairly strong under inclusion of uncertainties in prior odds.
item.dc:creator: Michael B. Weissman

item.title: A spatiotemporal Bayesian hierarchical model of heat-related mortality in Catalonia, Spain (2012--2022): The role of environmental and socioeconomic modifiers
item.description: arXiv:2511.17148v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Extreme heat represents a growing threat to public health as climate change intensifies. While its mortality impacts are well recognised, the interplay between heat, air pollution, and socioeconomic vulnerability remains insufficiently understood. We quantified the associations of extreme maximum temperatures and heatwaves with daily mortality in Catalonia (2012-2022) and evaluated how air pollutants-particularly ozone, nitrogen dioxide and particulate matter-and socioeconomic factors confound or modify this relationship. We conducted a time-series ecological analysis across 379 Basic Health Areas during summer months, linking mortality with meteorological, air pollution and socioeconomic indicators. Hierarchical Bayesian zero-inflated negative binomial models were fitted with nested spatiotemporal random effects (Mat\'ern SPDE field evolving over years; month nested within year; unstructured ABS frailty). Among 210.860 summer deaths in the complete environmental sample, extreme heat and heatwaves were associated with higher mortality after multi-pollutant and socioeconomic adjustment (e.g., extreme heat at lag 2: RR $1.105$, 95% CrI $1.086$-$1.125$; heatwave at lag 3: RR $1.142$, 95% CrI $1.116$-$1.167$; posterior Prob $\approx 1$). Ozone concentrations $\geq 100\,\mu$g/m$^3$ were positively associated with mortality, and extreme heat$\times$high ozone interactions further elevated risk. Areas with higher income inequality and older population structures also showed elevated mortality. These findings indicate that heat indicators raise summer mortality in Catalonia even after environmental and socioeconomic adjustment, while compound ozone exposure and contextual vulnerability further shape risk. Adaptation strategies should therefore combine heat-health warnings with air quality management and equity-oriented interventions.
item.dc:creator: David Solano, Marta Solans, Xavier Perafita, Anna Ruiz-Comellas, Marc Saez, Maria A. Barcel\'o

item.title: Phase Transitions in Collective Damage of Civil Structures under Natural Hazards
item.description: arXiv:2602.16195v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: The fate of cities under natural hazards depends not only on hazard intensity but also on the coupling of structural damage, a collective process that remains poorly understood. Here we show that urban structural damage exhibits phase-transition phenomena. As hazard intensity increases, the system can shift abruptly from a largely safe to a largely damaged state, analogous to a discontinuous phase transition in statistical physics. Higher diversity in the building portfolio smooths this transition, but multiscale damage clustering traps the system in a highly volatile regime that suppresses the emergence of predictable Gaussian statistics. The observed phenomenological patterns are interpreted through an effective random-field Ising model, with its key parameters translated into tangible engineering variables such as hazard demand, structural diversity, and modeling uncertainty. These insights establish a phase-aware description of collective damage, revealing that common engineering simplifications can distort the inherent phase of real urban portfolios. Critically, such phase distortions can substantially bias hazard loss estimates, producing relative errors of up to 50% in exceedance probabilities under moderate earthquakes---equivalent to a several-fold gap in anticipated repair costs. The phase-aware description turns the collective behavior of civil infrastructure damage into actionable diagnostics for urban risk assessment and planning.
item.dc:creator: Sebin Oh, Jinyan Zhao, Raul Rincon, Jamie E. Padgett, Ziqi Wang

item.title: Computing the final epidemic size distributions of a multi-type Galton--Watson process
item.description: arXiv:2606.03007v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We provide a theoretical ground to directly compute the final size distribution of a Galton--Watson process (GWP) from the implicit fixed point equations for its probability generating function (PGF). Firstly we show that valid identification of the final size PGF is ensured on any contour inside the unit polydisc. Furthermore, we derive error bounds for the PGF values on the contour, and establish the relationship between the differentiability of the offspring PGF and the final size PGF as a function of parameters that control the offspring distribution. Finally, we provide demonstrations using simulated and real-world data, and discuss potential identifiability issues regarding statistical inference that is associated with likelihoods that are not conditioned on extinction.
item.dc:creator: Yuta Okada, Hiroshi Nishiura

item.title: Can synthetic data reproduce real-world findings in epidemiology? A replication study using adversarial random forests
item.description: arXiv:2508.14936v4 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Synthetic data hold substantial potential to address practical challenges in epidemiology due to restricted data access and privacy concerns. However, many current methods suffer from limited quality, high computational demands, and complexity for non-experts. Furthermore, common evaluation strategies for synthetic data often fail to directly reflect statistical utility and measure privacy risks sufficiently. Against this background, a critical underexplored question is whether synthetic data can reliably reproduce key findings from epidemiological research while preserving privacy. We propose adversarial random forests (ARF) as an efficient and convenient method for synthesizing tabular epidemiological data. To evaluate its performance, we replicated statistical analyses from six epidemiological publications covering blood pressure, anthropometry, myocardial infarction, accelerometry, loneliness, and diabetes, from the German National Cohort (NAKO Gesundheitsstudie), the Bremen STEMI Registry U45 Study, and the Guelph Family Health Study. We further assessed how dataset dimensionality and variable complexity affect the quality of synthetic data, and contextualized ARF's performance by comparison with commonly used tabular data synthesizers in terms of utility, privacy, generalization, and runtime. Across all replicated studies, results on ARF-generated synthetic data consistently aligned with original findings. Even for datasets with relatively low sample size-to-dimensionality ratios, replication outcomes closely matched the original results across descriptive and inferential analyses. Reduced dimensionality and variable complexity further enhanced synthesis quality. ARF demonstrated favourable performance regarding utility, privacy preservation, and generalization relative to other synthesizers and superior computational efficiency.

item.title: Perceived vertical and eye level as one orientation process: a closed-form account of the Li-Matin combination rules for egocentric space
item.description: arXiv:2607.19681v4 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Li and Matin (2005a, 2005b) reported three regularities of the induced visually-perceived vertical (VPV), the direction judged upright. For small tilts, a peripheral line shifts it nearly linearly with tilt, two lines combine nearly linearly, and mirror-image tilts cancel. Each line votes at twice its angle, weighted by its strength. The votes' vector sum $c_1$ is the first circular moment of the doubled angles; half its angle, $\phi=\tfrac12\arg c_1$, is the induced vertical, a stimulus axis, not the judged upright. This is the orientation order-parameter model (PLUMB). We prove that $c_1$ is, up to a constant factor, the only additive summary of axes (lines without arrowheads) that scales with line strength and turns twice as far as the field rotates. With Li and Matin's own length gain and no per-configuration fit, the model matches their multiline coefficients in-sample. Their data rule out complete summation but not simple averaging for long lines. But a line's effect is fourfold (period $90^\circ$): it reverses past $45^\circ$ (Li and Matin, 2005a; Vingerhoets et al., 2009), and near-horizontal lines shift VPV as near-vertical ones do, which $c_1$ forbids. In a two-harmonic fit to Li and Matin's data, $c_1$ carries an estimated 2--4% of a near-vertical line's slope and a fourfold term the rest. To first order in tilt, for near-vertical segments, the readout equals the committee rule Shavit, Li, and Matin (2026) fit to eight line-array experiments, with its drives read as concentrations. If the half-fields' signals are read as sum and difference, perceived eye level (VPEL) is the difference, recovering Shavit, Li, and Matin's (2013) reversed integration rules; a fourfold term gives the same signals, so this does not single out $c_1$. Re-analysed data (30 observers) show the predicted signs and nulls, an internal check only; the cross-field gain is fitted.
item.dc:creator: A. Y. Shavit
